Stokes' theorem: surface S & boundary C
A thick tube winds twice across the box, doubling back on the left and passing both in front of and behind the z-axis. Drag to orbit — its only free edges are the far mouth (upper right) and the circle C facing you near the centre.

plan.contextChunk: This figure shows an oriented surface sitting inside a three-dimensional vector field, drawn within a thin blue wireframe box whose x, y, and z axes carry evenly spaced tick marks; x heads toward the lower left, y toward the lower right, and z upward. The surface is a thick blue-gray tube that winds and doubles back through the middle of the box, its lobes passing both in front of and behind the z axis so the shape overlaps itself. One end is an open circular mouth in the upper right region, and a second circular opening faces the viewer near the center. The letter S labels the tube body at its upper right lobe, and the letter C labels the boundary circle at the front-facing opening. Orange arrows of roughly equal length sit on a regular grid throughout the box and also lie directly across the tube, tilting up and to the right, with the tilt steepening at greater heights. Placing field arrows both in the surrounding space and on the surface itself lets the reader judge how the field meets the tube at each point. The arrangement poses a surface integral over a shape too convoluted to parameterize directly, motivating a route through the single labeled boundary curve instead.

elements: thin light-blue wireframe cube bounding the whole scene
black x-axis heading toward lower-left with evenly spaced tick marks and italic label 'x'
black y-axis heading toward lower-right with evenly spaced tick marks and italic label 'y'
black vertical z-axis with arrowhead at top and label 'z'
thick blue-gray tube surface S that winds and doubles back through the middle of the box, lobes passing both in front of and behind the z-axis so the shape overlaps itself
open circular mouth of the tube in the upper-right region (far end), shown as an ellipse with visible inner wall shading
front-facing circular opening near the center of the box, just right of the z-axis — the boundary curve C
label 'S' placed at the upper-right lobe of the tube
label 'C' placed just above/left of the front circular opening
regular 3D grid of short orange arrows of nearly equal length filling the box, tilting up and to the right with steeper tilt at greater heights
orange field arrows drawn directly on/through the tube surface so the field can be seen meeting the surface
(toggle-only) computed curl F arrows replacing the field arrows
(toggle-only) outward unit normal vectors n dS sampled on the tube surface
(toggle-only) oriented arrowheads around the boundary circle C indicating its direction of traversal

interactions.teaches: the tube really is a self-overlapping 3D surface — rotating shows which lobe passes in front of the z-axis and that the only free edge is the circle C plus the far mouth

interactions.label: Vectors shown
interactions.teaches: Stokes' theorem integrates curl F dotted with the surface normal, not the flux of F itself — the curl field points in a different direction than F and is what pairs with dS

interactions.label: Highlight
interactions.teaches: why a hopelessly convoluted surface integral can be replaced by a line integral: all the information Stokes' theorem needs lives on the single small oriented circle C

demo_steps.title: The surface in the field
demo_steps.narration: A blue-gray tube S winds through a box filled with a uniform-looking orange vector field F. Arrows also lie across the tube, so you can see how F meets the surface point by point.

demo_steps.title: Switch to curl F and the normal
demo_steps.narration: The orange arrows are replaced by curl F together with the outward normals n dS. The integrand of Stokes' theorem is curl F · n, which points quite differently from F itself.

demo_steps.title: Fade the surface, keep the boundary
demo_steps.narration: Dim the tube and highlight only the front circular opening C with its orientation arrows. The convoluted surface is nearly impossible to parameterize.

demo_steps.title: Stokes' trade
demo_steps.narration: Both shown together: the surface integral of curl F over all of S equals the line integral of F around the single small circle C — the hard object is traded for the easy one.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes:
World box: axis-aligned wireframe cube spanning x,y,z ∈ [-3,3] (edge 6 units), drawn as thin lines in light blue #5B9BD5 at ~1px. Axes are black lines through the origin extending to ±3.2 with small perpendicular tick marks every 0.5 unit; +x points toward screen lower-left, +y toward screen lower-right, +z straight up (standard isometric axonometric pose). Labels: italic 'x' at the lower-left end of the x-axis, italic 'y' at the lower-right end of the y-axis, 'z' at the top of the z-axis with an arrowhead.

Tube S: a tube of radius 0.35 swept along an open space curve that winds back on itself, e.g. r(t) = (1.9 cos t, 1.7 sin 2t, 0.55 sin t) for t ∈ [0.15, 2π+0.6] — the resulting shape has two lobes, one sweeping behind/above the z-axis toward the upper right of the frame and one sweeping in front/below toward the lower right, with the strands crossing near the z-axis so the tube visibly overlaps itself in the chosen view. Tube color blue-gray #6E7CA3 with lighter specular highlight #9AA6C4 and slightly darker interior wall #55618A; render double-sided so the open ends show inner wall.
Open far mouth: circular disc of radius 0.35 at the tube's far end, positioned in the upper-right region of the box (roughly x≈1.2, y≈1.8, z≈0.9), its plane roughly perpendicular to the tube axis so it reads as a tilted ellipse.
Boundary circle C: the near end of the tube, radius 0.35, centered just right of and slightly below the origin (roughly x≈0.1, y≈-0.2, z≈-0.35), its plane facing the viewer so it reads as a near-circular ellipse. Draw its rim as a thicker outlined ring.
Labels: 'S' in black ~0.3 units above-right of the upper-right lobe (near x≈1.1, y≈2.2, z≈1.3); 'C' in black just above-left of the front opening (near x≈-0.15, y≈-0.2, z≈0.15).

Vector field: F(x,y,z) = (1 + 0.25 z², 1, 0.4 + 0.4 z). Sampled on a 4×4×4 grid over [-2.5,2.5]³ plus extra samples placed on the tube surface. All arrows drawn at a fixed length ≈0.45 units (direction only, as in the source), orange #E8622A, cone head ~0.15 long. Because Fz grows with z and the horizontal components stay fixed, the arrows visibly tilt up and to the right more steeply near the top of the box — match that trend.
Curl mode: curl F = (0, 0.5 z, 0), drawn in a distinct warm color (#C0392B) with length proportional to |0.5 z| (clamped 0.15–0.5) so the arrows vanish near z=0 and lengthen toward the top and bottom; outward unit normals n on the tube drawn as short gray-green (#4C8C6B) arrows of length 0.35 at the same surface sample points, so the learner can compare curl F direction against n.
Boundary-emphasis mode: tube opacity drops to ~0.15, circle C rim drawn thick in #E8622A/gold with 6 small tangent arrowheads spaced around it showing counterclockwise orientation as seen from the viewer (consistent with the outward normal by the right-hand rule).
interactionPlan.notes: Build the tube with THREE.TubeGeometry on a CatmullRomCurve3 (or a Curve subclass evaluating the parametric formula), tubularSegments ≈ 400, radialSegments 24, closed:false, MeshStandardMaterial(side: DoubleSide, roughness 0.5, metalness 0.05) plus a hemisphere light and one directional key light from upper-left. Cap/ring meshes (THREE.CircleGeometry + torus rim) at both ends for the open mouths. Arrows as instanced cone+cylinder meshes or a pool of THREE.ArrowHelper reused between modes so toggling only updates directions/colors, not geometry counts. Wireframe box from THREE.LineSegments on BoxGeometry edges; ticks as tiny LineSegments. Labels ('x','y','z','S','C') as CSS2DRenderer sprites that always face the camera and stay legible during orbit. Use an orthographic camera in an isometric pose to match the axonometric look; OrbitControls with damping, no zoom past the box. Depth-sort correctly for the self-overlapping tube (depthWrite true, no transparency in default mode); when fading the tube for boundary emphasis, enable transparency and set depthWrite false so field arrows behind it remain visible.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between field F and curl F: the learner first sees the displayed orange vector field, then switches to a computed curl-vector overlay with the surface normal, making clear that the surface integral uses curl F dotted with dS rather than flux of F itself.
- Toggle between surface S and boundary C emphasis: the learner switches highlighting from the whole tube to the front circular boundary, making clear why Stokes' theorem can replace a difficult surface integral with information carried by the boundary curve.

authoredContext:
Calculate surface integral ∬ScurlF·dS, where S is the surface, oriented outward, in the figure and F=〈z,2xy,x+y〉.

A complicated surface in a vector field.

A diagram of a complicated surface S in a three dimensional vector field. The surface is a cylindrical tube that twists about in the three-dimensional space arbitrarily. The upper end of the tube is an open circle leading to inside the tube. It is centered on the z-axis at a height of z=1 and has a radius of 1. The bottom end of the tube is closed with a hemispherical cap on the end. The vector arrows are best described by their components. The x component is positive everywhere and becomes larger as z increases. The y component is positive in the first and third octants and negative in the other two. The z component is zero when y=x and becomes more positive with more positive x and y values and more negative in the other direction.

attempts.html:
Stokes' theorem: surface S & boundary C
Drag to orbit — see how the tube overlaps itself and that its only free edges are the far mouth and the circle C.
F = (1 + 0.25z², 1, 0.4 + 0.4z): arrows tilt up and to the right, more steeply high in the box.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Field arrows are drastically undersized — in the source the orange arrows are bold, clearly-directed darts filling the box, while in the render they read as tiny orange specks/dots, losing the vector-field impression entirely.

Arrow density/layout differs: source shows a dense field (roughly 7×7 per face plane) with arrows visibly on and around the tube; generated uses only a 4×4×4 grid plus 16 surface arrows, making the box look mostly empty.

Tube S is less convoluted and smaller relative to the box than in the source: the source shows two large interlocking lobes that overlap and pass over/under each other and nearly span the box width, the generated tube is a single thinner spiral occupying a smaller region.

In the source the tube's cross-sectional radius is noticeably thicker relative to its extent, and the dark inner-wall openings (far mouth and C) are prominent; in the render the openings are small and hard to read.

Camera is more corner-on (perfect hexagonal box silhouette) than the source, where the front face is nearly square with the x and y axes projecting at asymmetric angles — mildly changes the recognizable composition.
Tube shading is flatter/darker than the source's light blue-gray, glossy lobed surface, so occlusion cues between the overlapping lobes are weaker.
evaluation.notes: The core Stokes'-theorem composition (wireframe box, tick-marked axes, blue-gray tube S with boundary C, orange field) is present with genuinely useful interactions (F vs curl F·n, S/C highlighting, guided demo), but the vector field arrows are far too small and sparse to read as arrows and the tube is less convoluted and smaller than the source, weakening the visual match.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual structure is correct and interactions work; the issues are implementation details — arrow scale/density, tube thickness and convolution, shading, and camera angle — which are generator-level fixes.

Cap/ring meshes (THREE.CircleGeometry + torus rim) at both ends for the open mouths. Arrows as instanced cone+cylinder meshes or a pool of THREE.ArrowHelper reused between modes so toggling only updates directions/colors, not geometry counts. Depth-sort correctly for the self-overlapping tube (depthWrite true, no transparency in default mode); when fading the tube for boundary emphasis, enable transparency and set depthWrite false so field arrows behind it remain visible.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure shows an oriented surface sitting inside a three-dimensional vector field, drawn within a thin blue wireframe box whose x, y, and z axes carry evenly spaced tick marks; x heads toward the lower left, y toward the lower right, and z upward. The surface is a thick blue-gray tube that winds and doubles back through the middle of the box, its lobes passing both in front of and behind the z axis so the shape overlaps itself. One end is an open circular mouth in the upper right region, and a second circular opening faces the viewer near the center. The letter S labels the tube body at its upper right lobe, and the letter C labels the boundary circle at the front-facing opening. Orange arrows of roughly equal length sit on a regular grid throughout the box and also lie directly across the tube, tilting up and to the right, with the tilt steepening at greater heights. Placing field arrows both in the surrounding space and on the surface itself lets the reader judge how the field meets the tube at each point. The arrangement poses a surface integral over a shape too convoluted to parameterize directly, motivating a route through the single labeled boundary curve instead.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between field F and curl F: the learner first sees the displayed orange vector field, then switches to a computed curl-vector overlay with the surface normal, making clear that the surface integral uses curl F dotted with dS rather than flux of F itself.
- Toggle between surface S and boundary C emphasis: the learner switches highlighting from the whole tube to the front circular boundary, making clear why Stokes' theorem can replace a difficult surface integral with information carried by the boundary curve.

discrepancies: The tube S is far too small and too flat: in the source it sweeps across most of the box with two big lobes that fold back and visibly cross over/through themselves, whereas the generated tube is a thin, mostly planar hook confined near z≈0 and barely taller than its own diameter.

The characteristic self-overlap/occlusion of the source surface (one lobe passing in front of the other, with the inner wall of the far mouth clearly visible on the upper-left) is essentially absent, so the 'impossible to parameterize' visual message is weakened.
Vector field arrows in the generated figure are nearly horizontal pointing right; in the source they tilt noticeably up-and-to-the-right at roughly 30–45° across the whole box.
Arrow density/coverage is lower and more regular than the source's dense, evenly scattered field (source shows many more arrows, including several drawn crossing in front of the tube).
The boundary circle C is barely distinguishable — in the source it is a clearly drawn dark circular rim (mouth) near the centre with visible inner wall; here it reads as just the end of a thin tube.
Extra elements not in the source (green n dS normals, gold orientation arrows) appear under alternate modes; acceptable pedagogically but they go beyond the source figure.
evaluation.notes: Composition (wireframe box, ticked axes, orange field, blue-gray tube, S/C labels) and the interaction set are strong, but the surface itself is too small, too flat and lacks the dramatic self-overlapping double-lobe geometry that makes the source figure recognizable and makes the Stokes' theorem point.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual structure and interaction set are correct; the issues are concrete implementation details (tube scale/curvature and self-overlap, arrow direction/density, boundary circle emphasis) that can be fixed in rendering.

interactions.label: Vectors shown

interactions.teaches: why a hopelessly convoluted surface integral can be replaced by a line integral: all the information Stokes' theorem needs lives on the single small oriented circle C

demo_steps.title: The surface in the field
demo_steps.narration: A blue-gray tube S winds through a box filled with a uniform-looking orange vector field F. Arrows also lie across the tube, so you can see how F meets the surface point by point.

demo_steps.title: Switch to curl F and the normal
demo_steps.narration: The orange arrows are replaced by curl F together with the outward normals n dS. The integrand of Stokes' theorem is curl F · n, which points quite differently from F itself.

demo_steps.title: Fade the surface, keep the boundary
demo_steps.narration: Dim the tube and highlight only the front circular opening C with its orientation arrows. The convoluted surface is nearly impossible to parameterize.

demo_steps.title: Stokes' trade
demo_steps.narration: Both shown together: the surface integral of curl F over all of S equals the line integral of F around the single small circle C — the hard object is traded for the easy one.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes:
World box: axis-aligned wireframe cube spanning x,y,z ∈ [-3,3] (edge 6 units), drawn as thin lines in light blue #5B9BD5 at ~1px. Axes are black lines through the origin extending to ±3.2 with small perpendicular tick marks every 0.5 unit; +x points toward screen lower-left, +y toward screen lower-right, +z straight up (standard isometric axonometric pose). Labels: italic 'x' at the lower-left end of the x-axis, italic 'y' at the lower-right end of the y-axis, 'z' at the top of the z-axis with an arrowhead.

Tube S: a tube of radius 0.35 swept along an open space curve that winds back on itself, e.g. r(t) = (1.9 cos t, 1.7 sin 2t, 0.55 sin t) for t ∈ [0.15, 2π+0.6] — the resulting shape has two lobes, one sweeping behind/above the z-axis toward the upper right of the frame and one sweeping in front/below toward the lower right, with the strands crossing near the z-axis so the tube visibly overlaps itself in the chosen view. Tube color blue-gray #6E7CA3 with lighter specular highlight #9AA6C4 and slightly darker interior wall #55618A; render double-sided so the open ends show inner wall.
Open far mouth: circular disc of radius 0.35 at the tube's far end, positioned in the upper-right region of the box (roughly x≈1.2, y≈1.8, z≈0.9), its plane roughly perpendicular to the tube axis so it reads as a tilted ellipse.
Boundary circle C: the near end of the tube, radius 0.35, centered just right of and slightly below the origin (roughly x≈0.1, y≈-0.2, z≈-0.35), its plane facing the viewer so it reads as a near-circular ellipse. Draw its rim as a thicker outlined ring.
Labels: 'S' in black ~0.3 units above-right of the upper-right lobe (near x≈1.1, y≈2.2, z≈1.3); 'C' in black just above-left of the front opening (near x≈-0.15, y≈-0.2, z≈0.15).

Vector field: F(x,y,z) = (1 + 0.25 z², 1, 0.4 + 0.4 z). Sampled on a 4×4×4 grid over [-2.5,2.5]³ plus extra samples placed on the tube surface. All arrows drawn at a fixed length ≈0.45 units (direction only, as in the source), orange #E8622A, cone head ~0.15 long. Because Fz grows with z and the horizontal components stay fixed, the arrows visibly tilt up and to the right more steeply near the top of the box — match that trend.

attempts.html:
Stokes' theorem: surface S & boundary C
A thick tube winds twice across the box, doubling back on the left and passing both in front of and behind the z-axis. Drag to orbit — its only free edges are the far mouth (upper right) and the circle C facing you near the centre.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Tube geometry is simplified: the source S is a pretzel-like double-lobed tube with a clearly visible enclosed hole on the left loop and a strongly arched top band; the generated tube reads as a flatter single S-sweep with less self-overlap and much less vertical extent.
Far mouth of the tube is not visibly open — in the source the upper-right lobe end near the 'S' label shows a distinct elliptical opening; in the render it appears as a rounded, nearly closed cap.
Vector field is noticeably sparser than the source (4×4×4 grid vs. the dense field filling the box), so the box interior looks emptier than the original.

Axes are shorter than in the source: the z-axis in the original pierces the top of the box with an arrowhead well outside it, while here the axes terminate inside the wireframe, weakening the axis framing.

The tube in the source occupies a larger fraction of the box and clearly passes in front of and behind the z-axis with strong occlusion; the generated tube is smaller relative to the box and the crossings are less legible.
evaluation.notes: A well-composed, correctly-oriented recreation with the right primitives (wireframe box, ticked axes, orange field, blue-gray tube, S/C labels) and an unusually rich, functional interaction set; main weaknesses are a simplified, flatter tube that loses the source's pretzel double-lobe and open far mouth, a sparser arrow field, and a narration that claims C is the only boundary while the model actually has two free edges.
action_items: Reshape the tube curve to reproduce the source's two overlapping lobes with a visible hole on the left loop and greater z-amplitude, and cap/open the far mouth so its elliptical opening is clearly visible near the 'S' label.
Increase the field sampling (e.g. 5×5×5 or a jittered grid) so the box interior is filled with arrows at a density comparable to the source.
Extend the axes so their arrowheads protrude beyond the box faces as in the original, and enlarge the S and C labels slightly for a clearer hierarchy over the axis labels.
Fix the step-4 narration (or close the far mouth into an actual cap) so the statement that ∬_S curl F·n dS equals the single line integral around C is consistent with the surface's boundary.
